Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod is praised for what he has done for his people.1–7Their obligations to him.8–16
Praising the God who delivers (verses 1–7)

All the worship we can give God falls short of his excellence and of what we owe him—especially for redeeming us from sin and judgment.

Israel was commanded to remember God's mighty deeds through appointed public festivals.

To appreciate the greatness of a deliverance, we should remember how dreadful the danger or bondage was from which we were rescued.

We must not forget the degrading and ruinous slavery into which Satan, our oppressor, once brought us.

When distress of conscience drives us to cry to the Lord, he answers and sets us free.

Conviction of sin and the trials of affliction may become signs of his faithful concern for us.

If Israel remembered deliverance from Egypt on its feasts, how much more should Christians remember the greater redemption accomplished through Jesus Christ when gathering on the Christian Sabbath!

He has rescued us from a bondage far worse than Israel's slavery.

God calls his people to listen and obey (verses 8–16)

We should expect little from created things and much from the Creator.

By faith and prayer, we may receive from God everything truly necessary.

The wickedness of the world arises from human willfulness.

People refuse true religion because they do not want to submit to it.

God is not the author of their sin.

He leaves stubborn sinners to the desires of their own hearts and to their own plans. If they fail to do good, they must bear responsibility.

The Lord does not desire that any should perish.

What terrible enemies sinners become to themselves!

Sin prolongs our troubles and delays our enjoyment of salvation.

The fertile hills and fields of Canaan pictured spiritual and eternal blessings held through faith and obedience.

Christ is the Bread of Life, the Rock of salvation, and his promises are as sweet as honey to a godly soul.

But those who reject him as Lord and Master cannot expect to enjoy him as Savior and reward.
classic_reading:
[Ps.81.1-Ps.81.7]
Chapter 81
Chapter Outline
God is praised for what he has done for his people. | (1-7) |
Their obligations to him. | (8-16) |
Verses 1-7
All the worship we can render to the Lord is beneath his excellences, and our obligations to him, especially in our redemption from sin and wrath. What God had done on Israel's behalf, was kept in remembrance by public solemnities. To make a deliverance appear more gracious, more glorious, it is good to observe all that makes the trouble we are delivered from appear more grievous. We ought never to forget the base and ruinous drudgery to which Satan, our oppressor, brought us. But when, in distress of conscience, we are led to cry for deliverance, the Lord answers our prayers, and sets us at liberty. Convictions of sin, and trials by affliction, prove his regard to his people. If the Jews, on their solemn feast-days, were thus to call to mind their redemption out of Egypt, much more ought we, on the Christian sabbath, to call to mind a more glorious redemption, wrought out for us by our Lord Jesus Christ, from worse bondage.
[Ps.81.8-Ps.81.16]
Verses 8-16
We cannot look for too little from the creature, nor too much from the Creator. We may have enough from God, if we pray for it in faith. All the wickedness of the world is owing to man's wilfulness. People are not religious, because they will not be so. God is not the Author of their sin, he leaves them to the lusts of their own hearts, and the counsels of their own heads; if they do not well, the blame must be upon themselves. The Lord is unwilling that any should perish. What enemies sinners are to themselves! It is sin that makes our troubles long, and our salvation slow. Upon the same conditions of faith and obedience, do Christians hold those spiritual and eternal good things, which the pleasant fields and fertile hills of Canaan showed forth. Christ is the Bread of life; he is the Rock of salvation, and his promises are as honey to pious minds. But those who reject him as their Lord and Master, must also lose him as their Saviour and their reward.

Judges must govern for the public good (verses 1–5)

Magistrates have been entrusted with authority for the public good.

They serve God's Providence in maintaining order and peace, punishing wrongdoing and protecting people who act rightly.

God directs the decisions of rulers who desire justice and restrains those who intend evil.

We should acknowledge God's authority behind the offices and governors he permits to rule.

But when people responsible for justice twist it into wrongdoing, no good can be expected.

The wrong actions of public officials bring harm upon the public.

Every ruler will answer to God (verses 6–8)

Human beings find it difficult to receive honor and authority without becoming proud.

Yet all earthly rulers will die.

Every title and earthly dignity will be brought down into the dust.

God himself governs the world.

There is a righteous God to whom we may turn and on whom we may depend.

Henry also sees these words as pointing toward the Messiah's kingdom.

When we look at the world's disorder, we have good reason to pray that Jesus Christ will soon rule openly over every nation, bringing truth, righteousness and peace.
classic_reading:
[Ps.82.1-Ps.82.5]
Chapter 82
Chapter Outline
An exhortation to judges. | (1-5) |
The doom of evil rulers. | (6-8) |
Verses 1-5
Magistrates are the mighty in authority for the public good. Magistrates are the ministers of God's providence, for keeping up order and peace, and particularly in punishing evil-doers, and protecting those that do well. Good princes and good judges, who mean well, are under Divine direction; and bad ones, who mean ill, are under Divine restraint. The authority of God is to be submitted to, in those governors whom his providence places over us. But when justice is turned from what is right, no good can be expected. The evil actions of public persons are public mischiefs.
[Ps.82.6-Ps.82.8]
Verses 6-8
It is hard for men to have honour put upon them, and not to be proud of it. But all the rulers of the earth shall die, and all their honour shall be laid in the dust. God governs the world. There is a righteous God to whom we may go, and on whom we may depend. This also has respect to the kingdom of the Messiah. Considering the state of affairs in the world, we have need to pray that the Lord Jesus would speedily rule over all nations, in truth, righteousness, and peace.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe designs of the enemies of Israel.1–8Earnest prayer for their defeat.9–18
The enemies of God's people make plans (verses 1–8)

At times God seems not to be responding to unjust treatment of his people.

Then we may call upon him as the psalmist did.

All wicked people oppose God in some sense, and persecutors especially show themselves to be his enemies.

The Lord's people are his hidden ones.

The world does not truly know them, but he takes them under his special care.

If the enemies of the church can agree in their effort to destroy it, should not its friends unite in defending it?

Wicked people often wish religion would disappear from human society.

They would welcome the removal of every restraint it places upon their conduct, and would silence those who preach, profess and practice it.

They would go further if they had the power.

There have always been many enemies of God's church.

Their number makes the Lord's power in preserving a people for himself still more wonderful.

Prayer for God's judgment and enemies' repentance (verses 9–18)

Everyone who persists in opposing Christ's kingdom should take seriously the judgment described here.

God remains the same toward his people and toward those who attack them.

The psalm asks God to make the enemies' purposes as unstable as a turning wheel, and to scatter them like stubble.

It also uses the image of stubble consumed by fire to speak of final judgment.

But Henry makes an essential pastoral distinction:

We should desire no humiliation for our enemies or persecutors except what may help lead them to repentance and conversion.

The judgment of God will overtake those who continue to resist him unless they turn and seek the pardoning mercy of the Lord they have offended.

God's victories demonstrate that Jehovah possesses all power and perfection in himself.

Let us fear his judgment, surrender willingly to him and seek his mercy.

Above all, let us seek deliverance through the destruction of our own sinful fleshly desires, which fight against the soul.
classic_reading:
[Ps.83.1-Ps.83.8]
Chapter 83
Chapter Outline
The designs of the enemies of Israel. | (1-8) |
Earnest prayer for their defeat. | (9-18) |
Verses 1-8
Sometimes God seems not to be concerned at the unjust treatment of his people. But then we may call upon him, as the psalmist here. All wicked people are God's enemies, especially wicked persecutors. The Lord's people are his hidden one; the world knows them not. He takes them under his special protection. Do the enemies of the church act with one consent to destroy it, and shall not the friends of the church be united? Wicked men wish that there might be no religion among mankind. They would gladly see all its restraints shaken off, and all that preach, profess, or practise it, cut off. This they would bring to pass if it were in their power. The enemies of God's church have always been many: this magnifies the power of the Lord in preserving to himself a church in the world.
[Ps.83.9-Ps.83.18]
Verses 9-18
All who oppose the kingdom of Christ may here read their doom. God is the same still that ever he was; the same to his people, and the same against his and their enemies. God would make their enemies like a wheel; unsettled in all their counsels and resolves. Not only let them be driven away as stubble, but burnt as stubble. And this will be the end of wicked men. Let them be made to fear thy name, and perhaps that will bring them to seek thy name. We should desire no confusion to our enemies and persecutors but what may forward their conversion. The stormy tempest of Divine vengeance will overtake them, unless they repent and seek the pardoning mercy of their offended Lord. God's triumphs over his enemies, clearly prove that he is, according to his name JEHOVAH, an almighty Being, who has all power and perfection in himself. May we fear his wrath, and yield ourselves to be his willing servants. And let us seek deliverance by the destruction of our fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.

Longing for the Lord's house (verses 1–7)

God's appointed ordinances comfort believers in this troubled world.

Through them they enjoy the living God's presence.

That explains their sorrow when they cannot join in public worship.

These ordinances are to their souls what a nest is to a bird.

Yet their blessings are only an advance taste of the happiness of heaven.

How can people sincerely desire heaven's holy dwelling while complaining that worship here is wearying and unpleasant?

Truly happy people continue in the practice of true religion through the strength supplied by Jesus Christ.

Every part of our ability comes from him.

Pilgrims traveling toward the heavenly city may cross many valleys of tears and dry deserts.

But God opens wells of salvation and sends consolation to support them.

Those who press forward in Christian duty receive grace added to grace.

As they grow in grace now, they will eventually be made perfect in glory.

Seeking the God of worship (verses 8–12)

Whenever we approach God, we should ask him to look favorably upon Christ, his Anointed One, and receive us for Christ's sake.

Without the Mediator, we would not dare present ourselves before the Father.

But looking toward Christ in faith, we may confidently pray that God will regard us through him.

The psalmist loved God's ordinances.

We should regard one day in God's courts as better than a thousand elsewhere, and prefer the humblest duty in his service to the highest worldly promotion.

We live in darkness, but God is our Sun, giving light, life, guidance and direction.

We face dangers, but he is our Shield, protecting us from the fiery darts that surround us.

God has not promised riches and honors.

He has promised grace and glory to those who seek him through his appointed way.

Grace is heaven begun on earth through knowing, loving and serving God.

Glory is the completion of that blessedness: becoming like him and enjoying him fully forever.

Let us seek to walk uprightly and trust the Lord to provide everything that is truly good for us.

Even when we cannot go to the Lord's house, we may approach the Lord of the house through faith.

In him we can find genuine happiness and peace whatever our outward circumstances.
classic_reading:
[Ps.84.1-Ps.84.7]
Chapter 84
Chapter Outline
The psalmist expresses his affection to the ordinances of God. | (1-7) |
His desire towards the God of the ordinances. | (8-12) |
Verses 1-7
The ordinances of God are the believer's solace in this evil world; in them he enjoys the presence of the living God: this causes him to regret his absence from them. They are to his soul as the nest to the bird. Yet they are only an earnest of the happiness of heaven; but how can men desire to enter that holy habitation, who complain of Divine ordinances as wearisome? Those are truly happy, who go forth, and go on in the exercise of religion, in the strength of the grace of Jesus Christ, from whom all our sufficiency is. The pilgrims to the heavenly city may have to pass through many a valley of weeping, and many a thirsty desert; but wells of salvation shall be opened for them, and consolations sent for their support. Those that press forward in their Christian course, shall find God add grace to their graces. And those who grow in grace, shall be perfect in glory.
[Ps.84.8-Ps.84.12]
Verses 8-12
In all our addresses to God, we must desire that he would look on Christ, his Anointed One, and accept us for his sake: we must look to Him with faith, and then God will with favour look upon the face of the Anointed: we, without him, dare not show our faces. The psalmist pleads love to God's ordinances. Let us account one day in God's courts better than a thousand spent elsewhere; and deem the meanest place in his service preferable to the highest earthly preferment. We are here in darkness, but if God be our God, he will be to us a Sun, to enlighten and enliven us, to guide and direct us. We are here in danger, but he will be to us a Shield, to secure us from the fiery darts that fly thick about us. Through he has not promised to give riches and dignities, he has promised to give grace and glory to all that seek them in his appointed way. And what is grace, but heaven begun below, in the knowledge, love, and service of God? What is glory, but the completion of this happiness, in being made like to him, and in fully enjoying him for ever? Let it be our care to walk uprightly, and then let us trust God to give us every thing that is good for us. If we cannot go to the house of the Lord, we may go by faith to the Lord of the house; in him we shall be happy, and may be easy. That man is really happy, whatever his outward circumstances may be, who trusts in the Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPrayers for the continuance of former mercies.1–7Trust in God's goodness.8–13
Remembering mercy and seeking pardon (verses 1–7)

Present trouble should not make us forget God's earlier acts of mercy.

His favor is the source of happiness for nations and individuals alike.

When God forgives sin, he covers it completely.

Forgiveness is not a partial hiding of the transgressions of his people.

Christ, our Intercessor, stood on their behalf.

Because of his mediation, the Lord turned away his anger and showed compassion.

Only when we have been reconciled to God can we expect to enjoy the comfort of being reconciled to him.

Salvation flows from mercy alone.

When believers sin, they may experience severe and prolonged correction.

Yet when they humbly repent and pray, God can restore their joy in him.

God speaks peace through Christ (verses 8–13)

Sooner or later the Lord speaks peace to his people.

He may not give outward peace, but his Spirit can speak inwardly to their hearts.

This peace is promised to those who turn away from sin.

Every sin is folly, and backsliding is especially foolish because it means returning to wrongdoing once rejected.

Whatever our difficulties, God's salvation remains near.

His glory is also involved, so that honor may dwell among his people.

The truthfulness of God's promises appears in his mercy in sending the Redeemer.

Divine justice has been satisfied through the great atonement.

Christ, the Way, the Truth and the Life, came from the earth when he took our human nature.

The Father looked upon him with satisfaction.

For Christ's sake God grants every good thing, and especially the Holy Spirit, to those who ask.

Through Christ, forgiven sinners become fruitful in good works.

By looking to and trusting the Savior's righteousness, they find their feet established on the path of duty.

Righteousness guides them both in approaching God and in following him.
classic_reading:
[Ps.85.1-Ps.85.7]
Chapter 85
Chapter Outline
Prayers for the continuance of former mercies. | (1-7) |
Trust in God's goodness. | (8-13) |
Verses 1-7
The sense of present afflictions should not do away the remembrance of former mercies. The favour of God is the fountain of happiness to nations, as well as to particular persons. When God forgives sin, he covers it; and when he covers the sin of his people, he covers it all. See what the pardon of sin is. In compassion to us, when Christ our Intercessor has stood before thee, thou hast turned away thine anger. When we are reconciled to God, then, and not till then, we may expect the comfort of his being reconciled to us. He shows mercy to those to whom he grants salvation; for salvation is of mere mercy. The Lord's people may expect sharp and tedious afflictions when they commit sin; but when they return to him with humble prayer, he will make them again to rejoice in him.
[Ps.85.8-Ps.85.13]
Verses 8-13
Sooner or later, God will speak peace to his people. If he do not command outward peace, yet he will suggest inward peace; speaking to their hearts by his Spirit. Peace is spoken only to those who turn from sin. All sin is folly, especially backsliding; it is the greatest folly to return to sin. Surely God's salvation is nigh, whatever our difficulties and distresses are. Also, his honour is secured, that glory may dwell in our land. And the truth of the promises is shown by the Divine mercy in sending the Redeemer. The Divine justice is now satisfied by the great atonement. Christ, the way, truth, and life, sprang out of the earth when he took our nature upon him, and Divine justice looked upon him well pleased and satisfied. For his sake all good things, especially his Holy Spirit, are given to those who ask him. Through Christ, the pardoned sinner becomes fruitful in good works, and by looking to and trusting in the Saviour's righteousness, finds his feet set in the way of his steps. Righteousness is a sure guide, both in meeting God, and in following him

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist pleads his earnestness, and the mercy of God, as reasons why his prayer should be heard.1–7He renews his requests for help and comfort.8–17
Poverty, prayer, and divine mercy (verses 1–7)

When we recognize our poverty and misery, these needs become powerful reasons for approaching the throne of grace.

The safest way to preserve ourselves is to entrust ourselves to God's keeping.

The believer can appeal to the Lord as someone he has favored, set apart for himself, and made a participant in his sanctifying grace.

It is a great encouragement to prayer to know that God's converting grace has taught us to trust him and become his servants.

As we maintain fellowship with God, we may expect to receive comfort from him.

God's goodness is displayed in both giving and forgiving.

Whatever others may do, we should keep calling upon the Lord and commit our cause to him. We will not seek him in vain.

Asking to know God's way and receive his help (verses 8–17)

Our God alone possesses unlimited power and infinite love.

Christ is the Way and the Truth.

The believing soul wants to be taught God's truth and his ways, in order to walk in them, even more than it wants relief from earthly trouble.

Those who refuse to set the Lord before them pursue the souls of believers.

Yet the Lord's compassion, mercy and truth provide refuge and consolation.

People whose parents served the Lord may also mention that heritage when asking him to hear and help them.

As we consider David's experience and our own, we must not forget the One who was rich but became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty.
classic_reading:
[Ps.86.1-Ps.86.7]
Chapter 86
Chapter Outline
The psalmist pleads his earnestness, and the mercy of God, as reasons why his prayer should be heard. | (1-7) |
He renews his requests for help and comfort. | (8-17) |
Verses 1-7
Our poverty and wretchedness, when felt, powerfully plead in our behalf at the throne of grace. The best self-preservation is to commit ourselves to God's keeping. I am one whom thou favourest, hast set apart for thyself, and made partaker of sanctifying grace. It is a great encouragement to prayer, to feel that we have received the converting grace of God, have learned to trust in him, and to be his servants. We may expect comfort from God, when we keep up our communion with God. God's goodness appears in two things, in giving and forgiving. Whatever others do, let us call upon God, and commit our case to him; we shall not seek in vain.
[Ps.86.8-Ps.86.17]
Verses 8-17
Our God alone possesses almighty power and infinite love. Christ is the way and the truth. And the believing soul will be more desirous to be taught the way and the truth. And the believing soul will be more desirous to be taught the way and the truth of God, in order to walk therein, than to be delivered out of earthly distress. Those who set not the Lord before them, seek after believers' souls; but the compassion, mercy, and truth of God, will be their refuge and consolation. And those whose parents were the servants of the Lord, may urge this as a plea why he should hear and help them. In considering David's experience, and that of the believer, we must not lose sight of Him, who though he was rich, for our sakes became poor, that we through his poverty might be rich.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe glory of the church.1–3It is filled with the Divine blessing.4–7
Christ, the church's foundation (verses 1–3)

Christ himself is the foundation that God has laid for his church.

Holiness gives the church strength and stability.

We should not be ashamed of Christ's church, even when its outward condition is humble, or of the people who belong to it.

God has spoken glorious things about it.

No one can lay another foundation than Jesus Christ.

The glorious promises about Zion, spoken by the Spirit, point toward Christ and his work, the different offices he fulfills, the gospel church and its privileges and members, and finally heaven with its perfect happiness and glory.

The blessing of belonging to Zion (verses 4–7)

Christ's church is more glorious and excellent than any earthly nation.

The records of heaven include even the humblest person who has been born again.

When God judges everyone according to their works, he will take account of those who enjoyed the privileges of his sanctuary.

Much is required of those to whom much has been given.

Those who belong to Zion should remember their privileges and live consistently with their profession of faith.

The songs of Zion will be sung with joy and triumph.

Worldly-minded people look for happiness in wealth and pleasure.

But a soul transformed by grace finds its springs of joy in God's word and prayer.

Every grace and comfort flows from Christ through his appointed ordinances to believers' souls.
classic_reading:
[Ps.87.1-Ps.87.3]
Chapter 87
Chapter Outline
The glory of the church. | (1-3) |
It is filled with the Divine blessing. | (4-7) |
Verses 1-3
Christ himself is the Foundation of the church, which God has laid. Holiness is the strength and firmness of the church. Let us not be ashamed of the church of Christ in its meanest condition, nor of those that belong to it, since such glorious things are spoken of it. Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, even Jesus Christ. The glorious things spoken of Zion by the Spirit, were all typical of Christ, and his work and offices; of the gospel church, its privileges and members; of heaven, its glory and perfect happiness.
[Ps.87.4-Ps.87.7]
Verses 4-7
The church of Christ is more glorious and excellent than the nations of the earth. In the records of heaven, the meanest of those who are born again stand registered. When God renders to every man according to his works, he shall observe who enjoyed the privileges of his sanctuary. To them much was given, and of them much will be required. Let those that dwell in Zion, mark this, and live up to their profession. Zion's songs shall be sung with joy and triumph. The springs of the joy of a carnal worldling are in wealth and pleasure; but of a gracious soul, in the word of God and prayer. All grace and consolation are derived from Christ, through his ordinances, to the souls of believers.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist pours out his soul to God in lamentation.1–9He wrestles by faith, in his prayer to God for comfort.10–18
A believer's deeply troubled soul (verses 1–9)

The psalm's opening words are its only words of comfort and support.

Even godly people can suffer terribly. They may think very dark thoughts about their suffering and reach bleak conclusions about their future, because of melancholy and weakened faith.

The psalmist's greatest distress was his sense of God's displeasure.

Even those whom God loves may sometimes imagine themselves to be objects of his wrath.

No outward affliction is as painful as that fear.

The psalmist was probably describing his own troubles, but Henry also directs us to Christ.

We look to Jesus, wounded and bruised for our sins.

The divine wrath poured into his cup brought its greatest bitterness and weighed him down into darkness and the depths.

Continuing in prayer while comfort is delayed (verses 10–18)

Departed souls may declare God's faithfulness, justice and lovingkindness.

But dead bodies can neither enjoy his favors with comfort nor praise him in response.

The psalmist resolved to continue praying, especially because deliverance had not come quickly.

When our prayers are not answered soon, we must not abandon them.

The more severe our troubles, the more earnest and serious our prayers should be.

Nothing grieves God's child more than losing the sense of his presence; nothing is more frightening than the thought of being cast away from him.

When the sun is covered by clouds, the earth grows dark. If the sun left the earth entirely, it would become a dungeon.

Likewise, even people destined to experience God's favor may for a time feel his terrors.

The psalmist suffered that fear deeply.

When Providence or death separates us from friends, we rightly consider that loss an affliction.

This was the desperate condition of a godly person.

Yet Henry sees the psalm's appeals as particularly fitting to Jesus Christ.

We should not imagine that Jesus suffered for us only in Gethsemane and on Calvary.

His whole earthly life involved work and sorrow.

He endured unparalleled affliction from his youth onward and was prepared throughout life for the death he would eventually taste.

No other person could share the redemptive sufferings through which others would be saved.

When the hour came, everyone deserted him and fled.

Blessed Jesus, we often forsake you. Do not forsake us; do not take your Holy Spirit from us.
classic_reading:
[Ps.88.1-Ps.88.9]
Chapter 88
Chapter Outline
The psalmist pours out his soul to God in lamentation. | (1-9) |
He wrestles by faith, in his prayer to God for comfort. | (10-18) |
Verses 1-9
The first words of the psalmist are the only words of comfort and support in this psalm. Thus greatly may good men be afflicted, and such dismal thoughts may they have about their afflictions, and such dark conclusion may they make about their end, through the power of melancholy and the weakness of faith. He complained most of God's displeasure. Even the children of God's love may sometimes think themselves children of wrath and no outward trouble can be so hard upon them as that. Probably the psalmist described his own case, yet he leads to Christ. Thus are we called to look unto Jesus, wounded and bruised for our iniquities. But the wrath of God poured the greatest bitterness into his cup. This weighed him down into darkness and the deep.
[Ps.88.10-Ps.88.18]
Verses 10-18
Departed souls may declare God's faithfulness, justice, and lovingkindness; but deceased bodies can neither receive God's favours in comfort, nor return them in praise. The psalmist resolved to continue in prayer, and the more so, because deliverance did not come speedily. Though our prayers are not soon answered, yet we must not give over praying. The greater our troubles, the more earnest and serious we should be in prayer. Nothing grieves a child of God so much as losing sight of him; nor is there any thing he so much dreads as God's casting off his soul. If the sun be clouded, that darkens the earth; but if the sun should leave the earth, what a dungeon would it be! Even those designed for God's favours, may for a time suffer his terrors. See how deep those terrors wounded the psalmist. If friends are put far from us by providences, or death, we have reason to look upon it as affliction. Such was the calamitous state of a good man. But the pleas here used were peculiarly suited to Christ. And we are not to think that the holy Jesus suffered for us only at Gethsemane and on Calvary. His whole life was labour and sorrow; he was afflicted as never man was, from his youth up. He was prepared for that death of which he tasted through life. No man could share in the sufferings by which other men were to be redeemed. All forsook him, and fled. Oftentimes, blessed Jesus, do we forsake thee; but do not forsake us, O take not thy Holy Spirit from us.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's mercy and truth, and his covenant.1–4The glory and perfection of God.5–14The happiness of those in communion with him.15–18God's covenant with David, as a type of Christ.19–37A calamitous state lamented, Prayer for redress.38–52
God's unbreakable covenant (verses 1–4)

Our expectations may disappoint us, but God's promises remain established in heaven.

They belong to his eternal purposes and cannot be defeated by opponents on earth or in hell.

Trust in God's boundless mercy and everlasting truth can comfort us even through our deepest trials.

God's majesty, power and righteousness (verses 5–14)

The more we learn of God's works, the more reason we have to admire them.

True praise confesses that no one is like him.

Therefore our worship should be marked by reverence.

How little reverence is sometimes present in our congregations! We have reason to humble ourselves for that neglect.

The almighty power that struck Egypt will also defeat the church's enemies.

Those who trust God's mercy may rejoice in his name.

Mercy and truth direct all God's works. From his eternal counsel to the eternal results of his actions, everything rests upon justice and righteous judgment.

The joy of knowing God (verses 15–18)

Happy are those who truly know the joyful message of the gospel: they obey it, experience its power within their hearts and show its fruit in their lives.

Believers possess nothing in themselves, yet have everything in Christ Jesus, so they may rejoice in his name.

May the Lord enable us to do so.

Joy in the Lord strengthens his people.

Unbelief, by contrast, weakens our courage and discourages others. Though it can disguise itself as humility, it is actually a form of pride.

Christ is the Holy One of Israel. In him God's people are more blessed than through any other gift.

God's covenant with David points to Christ (verses 19–37)

The Lord anointed David with holy oil.

The anointing represented the grace and gifts David received, but it also pointed forward to Christ, the King, Priest and Prophet, who received the Holy Spirit without measure.

David was persecuted after being anointed, but his enemies were unable finally to overcome him.

Even this was only a faint picture of the Redeemer's suffering, rescue, glory and authority.

Only in Christ are the promises fully fulfilled.

He is the mighty God, the appointed Redeemer who alone can finish the work of our salvation.

We should seek assurance of our part in those blessings through the Holy Spirit's witness in our hearts.

David's descendants were corrected for their sins, and so are God's people.

But their correction is a rod, not a sword: it is intended to correct, not to destroy.

It rests in the hands of a wise and gracious Father who knows when discipline is necessary and what is best.

As the sun and moon remain in the heavens even when their appearance changes, God's covenant of grace in Christ remains secure despite changes in how his people experience it.

Lament, the cross, and continuing hope (verses 38–52)

At times God's providential dealings are difficult to reconcile with his promises.

Yet we know his works always fulfill his word.

When Christ himself hung upon the cross, it seemed as though God had rejected his Anointed One.

But the eternal covenant was not broken.

The honor of David's royal family faded. Crowns and thrones are easily brought into the dust.

Yet an unfading crown of glory awaits Christ's spiritual descendants.

Sin has brought devastation to many households, even distinguished families where true faith was once found.

Still, the Lord's unchanging truth and faithfulness reassure us that he will not finally reject the people he has chosen and brought into covenant with himself.

People mocked the faithful for serving God.

Likewise, the scoffers of the last days mock the Messiah's promised return (2 Peter 3:3–4).

God's dealings with David's household help us understand his dealings with believers and the church.

Their suffering may be terrible, but God will not finally abandon them.

Those who merely deceive themselves may misuse this promise, while other believers bring darkness and trouble upon themselves by careless living.

Yet true believers may rely on God's faithfulness as they perform their duties and bear the cross.

The psalm ends in praise despite its grief.

Those who thank God for his past actions may also thank him for what he will yet do.

The Lord will continue showing mercy to those who continue praising him.

God's mercy and truth, and his covenant. | (1-4) |
The glory and perfection of God. | (5-14) |
The happiness of those in communion with him. | (15-18) |
God's covenant with David, as a type of Christ. | (19-37) |

Verses 1-4
Though our expectations may be disappointed, yet God's promises are established in the heavens, in his eternal counsels; they are out of the reach of opposers in hell and earth. And faith in the boundless mercy and everlasting truth of God, may bring comfort even in the deepest trials.
[Ps.89.5-Ps.89.14]
Verses 5-14
The more God's works are known, the more they are admired. And to praise the Lord, is to acknowledge him to be such a one that there is none like him. Surely then we should feel and express reverence when we worship God. But how little of this appears in our congregations, and how much cause have we to humble ourselves on this account! That almighty power which smote Egypt, will scatter the enemies of the church, while all who trust in God's mercy will rejoice in his name; for mercy and truth direct all he does. His counsels from eternity, and their consequences to eternity, are all justice and judgment.
[Ps.89.15-Ps.89.18]
Verses 15-18
Happy are those who so know the joyful sound of the gospel as to obey it; who experience its power upon their hearts, and bring forth the fruit of it in their lives. Though believers are nothing in themselves, yet having all in Christ Jesus, they may rejoice in his name. May the Lord enable us to do so. The joy of the Lord is the strength of his people; whereas unbelief dispirits ourselves and discourages others. Though it steals upon us under a semblance of humility, yet it is the very essence of pride. Christ is the Holy One of Israel; and in him was that peculiar people more blessed than in any other blessing.
[Ps.89.19-Ps.89.37]
Verses 19-37
The Lord anointed David with the holy oil, not only as an emblem of the graces and gifts he received, but as a type of Christ, the King Priest, and Prophet, anointed with the Holy Ghost without measure. David after his anointing, was persecuted, but none could gain advantage against him. Yet all this was a faint shadow of the Redeemer's sufferings, deliverance, glory, and authority, in whom alone these predictions and promises are fully brought to pass. He is the mighty God. This is the Redeemer appointed for us, who alone is able to complete the work of our salvation. Let us seek an interest in these blessings, by the witness of the Holy Spirit in our hearts. As the Lord corrected the posterity of David for their transgressions, so his people shall be corrected for their sins. Yet it is but a rod, not a sword; it is to correct, not to destroy. It is a rod in the hand of God, who is wise, and knows what he does; gracious, and will do what is best. It is a rod which they shall never feel, but when there is need. As the sun and moon remain in heaven, whatever changes there seem to be in them, and again appear in due season; so the covenant of grace made in Christ, whatever alteration seems to come to it, should not be questioned.
[Ps.89.38-Ps.89.52]
Verses 38-52
Sometimes it is not easy to reconcile God's providences with his promises, yet we are sure that God's works fulfil his word. When the great Anointed One, Christ himself, was upon the cross, God seemed to have cast him off, yet did not make void his covenant, for that was established for ever. The honour of the house of David was lost. Thrones and crowns are often laid in the dust; but there is a crown of glory reserved for Christ's spiritual seed, which fadeth not away. From all this complaint learn what work sin makes with families, noble families, with families in which religion has appeared. They plead with God for mercy. God's unchangeableness and faithfulness assure us that He will not cast off those whom he has chosen and covenanted with. They were reproached for serving him. The scoffers of the latter days, in like manner, reproach the footsteps of the Messiah when they ask, Where is the promise of his coming? [2Pet.3.3] 2Pe 3:3, [2Pet.3.4] 4. The records of the Lord's dealings with the family of David, show us his dealings with his church, and with believers. Their afflictions and distresses may be grievous, but he will not finally cast them off. Self-deceivers abuse this doctrine, and others by a careless walk bring themselves into darkness and distress; yet let the true believer rely on it for encouragement in the path of duty, and in bearing the cross. The psalm ends with praise, even after this sad complaint. Those who give God thanks for what he has done, may give him thanks for what he will do. God will follow those with his mercies, who follow him with praises.

The eternal God and our brief lives (verses 1–6)

Henry supposes this psalm concerns the judgment pronounced upon Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14).

God's favor and protection are the only lasting refuge and comfort for our souls in this troubled world.

Christ Jesus is the dwelling place and refuge to whom we may always turn.

Our lives are passing away, and every earthly comfort is temporary.

But God lives forever, and believers discover his faithfulness.

When sickness or suffering brings us close to death, God calls us to turn back to him through repentance and a renewed life.

A thousand years count for nothing beside his eternity.

There is some relationship between one minute and a million years, but no comparable measure between time and eternity.

The events of a thousand years, whether past or future, are more fully present to the eternal mind of God than yesterday's events are to ours.

At the resurrection, body and soul will be reunited.

Time slips past almost unnoticed, as when people sleep.

Life resembles floodwater that passes quickly.

We flourish briefly like grass.

Old age may cause us to wither gradually, or illness and disaster may cut us down suddenly.

Receiving God's discipline with reverence (verses 7–11)

The trials of God's people often arise from his fatherly love.

But the judgments of sinners—and believers' chastisements for particular sins—must also be recognized as signs of his displeasure toward wrongdoing.

God knows every secret sin. No one succeeds in hiding transgression from him.

Our years cannot be recalled any more than words already spoken.

Life is marked by toil and trouble, and it may be cut short in the years we expected to enjoy.

We should therefore stand in awe before God.

Fallen angels know his anger.

Sinners undergoing final judgment know it.

Yet who among us can fully describe its power?

Few consider it seriously enough.

Those who mock sin or take Christ lightly do not understand divine judgment.

Who can endure that consuming fire?

Asking for wisdom and enduring mercy (verses 12–17)

To gain true wisdom, we must ask God to teach us through the Holy Spirit.

We need his instruction and the comfort and joy that accompany renewed assurance of his favor.

We appeal to mercy, not to any merit of our own.

God's favor is a fountain of lasting joy and can more than compensate for past suffering.

May grace within us produce good works, and may divine comfort bring gladness to our hearts and faces.

We ask God to establish the work of our hands—and, in order for that work to stand, to establish us in it.

Do not waste these brief precious days pursuing fantasies that leave us spiritually poor.

Seek instead forgiveness of sins and the heavenly inheritance.

Pray that the Holy Spirit will convert our hearts and that the beauty of holiness will be visible in our behavior.
classic_reading:
[Ps.90.1-Ps.90.6]
Chapter 90
Chapter Outline
The eternity of God, the frailty of man. | (1-6) |
Submission to Divine chastisements. | (7-11) |
Prayer for mercy and grace. | (12-17) |
Verses 1-6
It is supposed that this psalm refers to the sentence passed on Israel in the wilderness, Nu 14. The favour and protection of God are the only sure rest and comfort of the soul in this evil world. Christ Jesus is the refuge and dwelling-place to which we may repair. We are dying creatures, all our comforts in the world are dying comforts, but God is an ever-living God, and believers find him so. When God, by sickness, or other afflictions, turns men to destruction, he thereby calls men to return unto him to repent of their sins, and live a new life. A thousand years are nothing to God's eternity: between a minute and a million of years there is some proportion; between time and eternity there is none. All the events of a thousand years, whether past or to come, are more present to the Eternal Mind, than what was done in the last hour is to us. And in the resurrection, the body and soul shall both return and be united again. Time passes unobserved by us, as with men asleep; and when it is past, it is as nothing. It is a short and quickly-passing life, as the waters of a flood. Man does but flourish as the grass, which, when the winter of old age comes, will wither; but he may be mown down by disease or disaster.
[Ps.90.7-Ps.90.11]
Verses 7-11
The afflictions of the saints often come from God's love; but the rebukes of sinners, and of believers for their sins, must be seen coming from the displeasure of God. Secret sins are known to God, and shall be reckoned for. See the folly of those who go about to cover their sins, for they cannot do so. Our years, when gone, can no more be recalled than the words that we have spoken. Our whole life is toilsome and troublesome; and perhaps, in the midst of the years we count upon, it is cut off. We are taught by all this to stand in awe. The angels that sinned know the power of God's anger; sinners in hell know it; but which of us can fully describe it? Few seriously consider it as they ought. Those who make a mock at sin, and make light of Christ, surely do not know the power of God's anger. Who among us can dwell with that devouring fire?
[Ps.90.12-Ps.90.17]
Verses 12-17
Those who would learn true wisdom, must pray for Divine instruction, must beg to be taught by the Holy Spirit; and for comfort and joy in the returns of God's favour. They pray for the mercy of God, for they pretend not to plead any merit of their own. His favour would be a full fountain of future joys. It would be a sufficient balance to former griefs. Let the grace of God in us produce the light of good works. And let Divine consolations put gladness into our hearts, and a lustre upon our countenances. The work of our hands, establish thou it; and, in order to that, establish us in it. Instead of wasting our precious, fleeting days in pursuing fancies, which leave the possessors for ever poor, let us seek the forgiveness of sins, and an inheritance in heaven. Let us pray that the work of the Holy Spirit may appear in converting our hearts, and that the beauty of holiness may be seen in our conduct.
